evidence: src/application/order-service.ts: private requireProduct(id) { const product = this.products.findById(id); if (!product) throw new DomainError("PRODUCT_NOT_FOUND", `Product ${id} does not exist.`); return product; }

src/application/order-service.ts: placeOrder repeats this inline: const product = this.products.findById(item.productId); if (!product) { throw new DomainError("PRODUCT_NOT_FOUND", `Product ${item.productId} does not exist.`); }
src/application/order-service.ts: cancelOrder uses the helper: order.items.forEach((item) => this.requireProduct(item.productId).release(item.quantity))

src/application/order-service.ts: placeOrder checks stock itself (item.quantity > product.availableStock → INSUFFICIENT_STOCK) before calling products[index].reserve(item.quantity), so the stock rule may also be enforced inside Product.reserve (not visible)
parsedVerdict.reasoning: The unit is a single file, src/application/order-service.ts, and it mostly serves one concern: the order and inventory use cases behind OrderService, built on domain repositories, entities and DomainError. One part breaks the rubric. The file defines a private helper, requireProduct(id), to look up a product and throw DomainError("PRODUCT_NOT_FOUND", ...) if it is missing. cancelOrder uses this helper, but placeOrder repeats the same lookup and throw inline in its items.map callback, with the same error code and message. That puts the product-must-exist rule in two places in the same class and bypasses the module's own helper. A change to that rule, such as a new error message or code, would have to be made in both places. A smaller point: placeOrder also checks item.quantity > product.availableStock before calling product.reserve. Product.reserve probably enforces the same rule, but that file is not shown, so this is not cited as a violation; the comment shows the pre-check is deliberate. Putting addProduct and listProducts in OrderService is a mild mix of product-catalogue and order concerns, but they are closely related and not enough to fail the unit on their own. The verdict rests on the duplicated lookup and the bypass of requireProduct.
